questions.q: Orders are sorted by id. You need the first order whose customer name is "Bola Ade". Which search fits?
questions.explain: Binary search only works on the key the data is sorted by. The names are in no particular order, so you have to look at each order: O(n). Sorting by name first would cost more than one scan.
options: Linear search, because the orders are not sorted by name

questions.q: When does linear search do the most work?
questions.explain: It stops at the first match, so a missing item means looking at all n items. That is the case a support tool hits every time someone mistypes an id.
options: When the item is at the front
When the item is exactly in the middle
When the item is at the end or not present at all

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: find returns the first match, findLast searches from the end. When nothing matches, findIndex returns −1 and find returns undefined. Both must be checked by the caller.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: indexOf compares with ===, and NaN === NaN is false, so it never finds NaN. includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to itself. A predicate with Number.isNaN finds it too.
questions.code:
const ratings = [4, NaN, 5];
console.log(ratings.indexOf(NaN), ratings.includes(NaN), ratings.findIndex(Number.isNaN));

questions.q: A support tool forgets to check the "not found" result. What does this print?
questions.explain: findIndex returns −1, orders[-1] is undefined (negative indexes are not "from the end" with brackets), and reading .total of undefined throws. The crash happens one step away from the real mistake: not handling −1.

questions.q: What must be true for binary search to give correct answers?
questions.explain: Binary search throws away half the array based on one comparison, which is only valid if everything on that side is also smaller (or larger). Duplicates and strings are fine; unsorted data gives silent wrong answers.
options: The array must have an odd length
The array must be sorted by the same key and comparison the search uses

questions.q: A sorted array holds 1,000,000 order ids. At most how many items does binary search look at?
questions.explain: Each look halves the remaining range, so after k looks at most n / 2k remain. 220 is just over a million, so 20 looks always suffice. Doubling the data adds one look.

questions.q: What is the loop invariant of the inclusive binary search (lo = 0, hi = length − 1, while (lo <= hi))?
questions.explain: Every line follows from this. Moving lo to mid + 1 is allowed because everything up to mid is too small; when lo > hi, the range is empty, so the target is absent.
options: If the target is in the array, its index is between lo and hi, inclusive
The range halves exactly every step

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: First mid is index 3 (1020), too small, so lo = 4. Next mid is floor((4 + 6) / 2) = 5, which holds 1047. Two looks.

questions.q: Binary search for a missing id. Where do lo and hi end up?
questions.explain: The loop ends with lo = hi + 1. lo (3) is exactly where 1018 would be inserted to keep the array sorted: between 1015 and 1020. That is the idea behind lower bound.

questions.q: How much stack does recursive binary search use on n items?
questions.explain: Each call handles half the previous range, so the depth is about log₂ n: 21 frames for a million items. That is harmless, unlike recursion on a deep chain. JavaScript engines do not eliminate the tail calls, so the frames really are kept.
options: O(log n), one frame per halving

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For 800: mids 3 (4000), 1 (1200), 0 (800): 3 looks. For 99,999: mids 3, 5 (12000), 6 (45000), 7 (150000), then the range is empty: 4 looks. Neither is more than ⌊log₂ 8⌋ + 1 = 4.
options:
found at 0 after 3 looks
missing after 4 looks

found at 0 after 1 looks
missing after 8 looks

found at 0 after 4 looks
missing after 3 looks

found at 0 after 3 looks
missing after 3 looks

questions.q: This version uses while (lo < hi) with an inclusive hi. What does it print?
questions.explain: 1011 is found at the first middle. For 1004 and 1015 the range shrinks to a single index (lo === hi) and the loop stops without looking at it. A one-item array never enters the loop at all.

questions.q: A binary search uses lo = mid (instead of mid + 1) with while (lo <= hi). What happens when lo and hi are neighbours and the target is larger than items[lo]?
questions.explain: With lo = 2 and hi = 3, mid = 2; setting lo = 2 again is no progress. Every branch must shrink the range. It only happens for some targets, so a few happy-path tests can miss it.
options: It finds the target one step later
mid rounds down to lo, so lo = mid changes nothing and the loop never ends

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: (1 + 2) / 2 is 1.5, and ids[1.5] looks up a property named "1.5", which does not exist. Always floor the middle.

questions.q: Binary searching over large numbers (for example byte offsets in a big log file). What does this print?
questions.explain: Bitwise operators convert their operands to 32-bit signed integers, and 5,000,000,010 does not fit: it wraps around to 705,032,714, so >> 1 produces a "middle" that is not even inside the range. Math.floor(x / 2) works on all integers up to 253.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: sort() without a comparator compares as text, so "800" sorts after "150000". The search sees 150000 at the middle, goes left, and never reaches the 800 on the right. Sort numbers with (a, b) => a - b.

questions.q: The id arrives from a form as the string "734512". The orders' ids are numbers. What does a ===-based binary search return, and why?
questions.explain: Mixed types make the comparisons disagree with each other. Convert and validate input at the boundary (Number(text), Number.isInteger) so the search only ever sees the type it was written for.
options: The right index, because JavaScript converts types
−1: < converts the string and narrows to the right place, but === never matches a number
The index of the first order

questions.q: A sorted price list contains ₦12,000 five times. Which index does plain binary search return for 12,000?
questions.explain: Plain binary search stops at any match. To get the first occurrence use lower bound; for one past the last, upper bound.
options: Always the first of the five
Always the last of the five
Whichever of the five it lands on first; not necessarily the first or the last

questions.q: What does lowerBound(items, target) return?
questions.explain: If the target is present, that is its first occurrence; if not, it is where the target would be inserted. It never returns −1: "past the end" is items.length.
options: The index of the largest item smaller than the target
The first index whose item is greater than or equal to the target, or items.length if there is none
The first index whose item is strictly greater than the target

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first 1200 is at index 1; the first item greater than 1200 is at 4, so there are 4 − 1 = 3 of them. 3000 would go at index 4. Nothing is greater than 9000, so the upper bound is the length, 6.

questions.q: In lowerBound, while (lo < hi) and hi = mid are correct, yet the same two lines were bugs in the inclusive binary search. Why?
questions.explain: Each style is consistent with its own meaning of hi. The bugs come from mixing them: an inclusive hi with an exclusive loop condition, or an exclusive update with an inclusive range.
options: Lower bound never needs to terminate
hi is exclusive here (starts at items.length), so lo === hi means an empty range and hi = mid still shrinks it
Because lower bound only works on unique items
They are bugs in both; lower bound just rarely hits them

questions.q: How do you count the sorted prices between ₦10,000 and ₦50,000 inclusive?
questions.explain: lowerBound(10000) is the first price ≥ 10,000, and upperBound(50000) is the first price > 50,000. Everything in between is in the range, both ends included.

questions.q: You keep an array sorted by inserting each new order at lowerBound(orders, id) with splice. What does each insert cost?
questions.explain: Binary search only finds the position. Making room in an array moves elements. That trade-off is why balanced search trees exist, and why sorted arrays suit data that is read far more often than it changes.
options: O(n): finding the spot is O(log n), but splice shifts every later element
O(n log n), because the array is re-sorted

questions.q: Orders are sorted by ISO timestamp. To get every order on 3 September, which pair of searches is safest?
questions.explain: A half-open range [start of day, start of next day) catches everything, including 23:59:59.5, without inventing a "last moment of the day". It is the same reasoning as WHERE placed_at >= … AND placed_at < … in SQL.
options: A binary search for "2026-09-03", then scan both ways
Linear search for timestamps starting with "2026-09-03"

questions.q: ISO timestamps are compared as strings. What does this print?
questions.explain: ISO strings put the largest unit first and use fixed widths, so string order equals time order. Locale formats do not: "9/…" sorts after "1…" as text. Store and compare timestamps in ISO form (or as numbers), never in display formats.

questions.q: Names are sorted. Why does lowerBound(names, "ora") find the first name starting with "ora"?
questions.explain: In sorted order, all strings with a given prefix are contiguous, and the prefix itself sorts just before them. Read forward from the lower bound while the prefix matches: O(L log n + k).
options: Every name starting with "ora" is ≥ "ora" and sorts before any larger name without that prefix, so they form one block that starts at the lower bound
It only works if exactly one name has that prefix
Because strings are compared by length

questions.q: You have 100,000 unsorted order totals and will run 5 searches. Should you sort first?
questions.explain: Sorting costs about n log₂ n. It pays off once the number of searches exceeds roughly 2 log₂ n (a few dozen here). For a handful of searches, scan.
options: Yes, always: binary search is faster
No: 5 linear searches cost about 5 × 50,000 comparisons, less than the roughly 1.7 million a sort needs
No, because binary search cannot handle 100,000 items

questions.q: A service needs "get order by id" (millions of times) and "all orders in this id range" (occasionally). The data changes once a day. What fits best?
questions.explain: A Map gives O(1) exact lookups but cannot answer ranges without a scan. A sorted array answers both in O(log n) and is rebuilt cheaply once a day. Keeping both trades memory for the fastest exact lookups.
options: A sorted array for ranges, optionally with a Map for the exact lookups
A trie of the ids as strings

questions.q: A test for binary search asserts binarySearch([5, 7, 7, 7, 9], 7) === 1. What is wrong with it?
questions.explain: A test must check the contract, not one implementation's behaviour. Plain binary search promises some matching index. If you need the first, test lower bound for that.
options: Nothing; index 1 is the only correct answer
Binary search may correctly return 1, 2 or 3; the test should accept any index that holds 7
Binary search cannot be tested with duplicates

questions.q: Which set of inputs is most likely to expose a binary search bug?
questions.explain: Binary search bugs live at the edges of the range. A target in the middle of a big array is found by almost any broken version; one-element and boundary cases are where off-by-one errors show.
options: A sorted array of 1,000 random numbers and a target in the middle
The empty array, one element, targets below the minimum and above the maximum, and runs of duplicates

questions.q: Why is "the next 50 orders after id 734,512" (WHERE id > 734512 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50) better than OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 50 for deep pages?
questions.explain: Cursor pagination jumps straight to the position with the index, then reads forward, like upperBound followed by a slice. OFFSET counts rows from the start every time.
options: The id condition is a lower-bound search in the index, O(log n), while OFFSET must walk past 500,000 rows, and shifts when new orders arrive
The id version returns more rows

questions.q: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 1,000 commits. About how many test runs does git bisect need to find the commit?
questions.explain: Each test run tells you whether the bug is before or after the middle commit, halving the range: log₂ 1,000 ≈ 10. It is binary search over history, and it relies on the same precondition: once the bug appears, it stays.

questions.q: Finish firstOver(orders, kobo): return the id of the first order whose total is greater than kobo, or null if there is none, using a plain loop that stops early. It should print 1043 null.
questions.explain: Return as soon as a match is found; return an explicit "not found" value after the loop. orders.find((o) => o.kobo > kobo)?.id ?? null does the same in one line. O(n).

questions.q: Finish binarySearch(ids, target), iteratively, with an inclusive range. Return the index or −1. It should print 0 4 9 -1 -1 -1.
questions.explain: Invariant: if the target exists, it is in lo..hi. Inclusive hi needs lo <= hi, and both updates exclude mid so the range always shrinks. The tests cover the first item, the last, a gap and both outside ends.

questions.q: Finish the recursive findOrder(orders, id, lo, hi): search orders sorted by id and return the order's customer, or null. It should print Chioma null Ada.
questions.explain: The base case is the empty range; each recursive call searches one half. Remember to return the recursive call's result, a common slip that makes every search return undefined.

questions.q: Finish lowerBound(items, target) with a half-open range: return the first index whose item is ≥ target, or items.length. It should print 0 1 1 4 6.
questions.explain: Invariant: everything before lo is smaller than the target, everything from hi on is ≥ it. When they meet, that index is the answer. 1200 returns its first occurrence; 20000 returns the length (insert at the end).

questions.q: Using the given lowerBound and upperBound, finish countBetween(prices, low, high) (inclusive) and countEqual(prices, value). It should print 4 3 0.
questions.explain: An inclusive range [low, high] is upperBound(high) − lowerBound(low), and "equal to v" is the range [v, v]. Two binary searches: O(log n), however many items match.

questions.q: Exchange rates are sorted by the date they took effect. Finish rateOn(rates, date): return the rate of the last change on or before date, or null if none, with a binary search (upper bound minus one). It should print null 1520 1520 1610.
questions.explain: Upper bound finds the first change strictly after the date; the one before it is the last change on or before it. A change on exactly that date applies, which is why the comparison is <=. Upper bound 0 means no change had happened yet.

questions.q: Finish firstAndLast(sorted, value): return [first, last] indexes of value, or [-1, -1], in O(log n). It should print 1,3 5,5 -1,-1.
questions.explain: The first occurrence is the lower bound, the last is upper bound minus one. If they coincide, the value is absent. A linear scan outward from any match would be O(n) when the value repeats many times.

questions.q: This binary search hangs for some targets and misses others. Fix it (keep the inclusive range) so it prints 0 1 2 3 -1 -1.
questions.explain: Three fixes, all from the invariant: an inclusive range must loop while lo <= hi, and both updates must exclude mid (mid + 1, mid − 1) so the range shrinks every time.
